nodes.label: Fundamentals and Maxims of Equity
nodes.summary: Jurisdiction of equity, the core maxims guiding equitable relief, the conscience-based jurisdiction, and the relationship between equity and common law in Hong Kong.

nodes.label: The Role of Equity
nodes.summary: Equity acts in personam on the conscience of the legal owner to prevent unconscionable conduct. It supplements the common law but does not override it.

nodes.label: Equity Follows the Law
nodes.summary: Equity recognises legal rights and interests unless there is a reason to intervene. It does not override common law but acts upon the conscience of the legal title holder.

nodes.label: Equity Acts on the Conscience
nodes.summary: The touchstone of equitable jurisdiction is the defendant's unconscionable behaviour. Equity intervenes where it would be unconscionable for the legal owner to insist on their strict legal rights.

nodes.label: Core Maxims Overview
nodes.summary: The maxims are flexible principles, not rigid rules, but guide the exercise of equitable jurisdiction. They are applied in the context of the particular case.

nodes.label: He Who Seeks Equity Must Do Equity
nodes.summary: A claimant must fulfil their own future obligations to obtain equitable relief. The court will not grant a remedy if the claimant will not act equitably.

nodes.label: Clean Hands
nodes.summary: A party seeking equitable relief must not have acted improperly in relation to the subject matter of the claim. The misconduct must have a direct connection to the transaction.

nodes.label: Equity Regards as Done That Which Ought to Be Done
nodes.summary: An enforceable obligation is treated as performed. Most commonly applied in contracts for the sale of land and agreements for leases.

nodes.label: Equity Will Not Assist a Volunteer / Perfect an Imperfect Gift
nodes.summary: Equity will not help a donee who has given no consideration to complete an imperfect gift. The donor must have done everything necessary to transfer legal title.

nodes.label: Delay Defeats Equity (Laches / Acquiescence)
nodes.summary: A party who sleeps on their rights and unreasonably delays bringing a claim may be barred by laches or acquiescence. The court considers the length of delay, prejudice caused, and whether the party knowingly stood by.

nodes.label: Earl of Oxford's Case (1615) 1 Ch Rep 1
nodes.summary: Foundational authority: where equity and common law conflict, equity prevails. Equity acts in personam on the conscience.

nodes.label: Ng Yat Chi v Max Share Ltd [2005] 2 HKLRD 1 (CFA)
nodes.summary: Maxim: he who seeks equity must do equity. A petitioner abusing his position to defraud a company cannot rely on mutual confidence to obtain a winding-up order.

nodes.label: Li Hung Chan v Wong Woon Heung [1994] 1 HKLR 265 (CA)
nodes.summary: Clean hands maxim: husband who assigned property to concubine to defeat creditors could not claim she held it on trust for him.

nodes.label: Walsh v Lonsdale (1882) 21 ChD 9
nodes.summary: Equity regards as done that which ought to be done: an agreement for a lease is as good as a formal lease in equity.

nodes.label: Wu Koon Tai v Wu Yau Loi [1997] 2 HKC 154
nodes.summary: Imperfect gift: unregistered successor who sold land failed to pass legal title. Equity will not perfect an imperfect gift.

nodes.label: Official Administrator v The Luk Hoi Tong Co Ltd [2003] 2 HKLRD 31
nodes.summary: Imperfect gift: mere deposit of share certificates and seal without executed transfer forms was an imperfect gift; equity does not perfect it.
